SUMMARY OF ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF CITING/REFEREE’S REPORT/INCIDENT FOOTAGE
At the 52nd minute of the match, a Red Card was issued against the Player for a breach of Law 9.11
(reckless or dangerous action):
“Following a review from the TMO, it was established that the player intentionally kicked an opponent
in the face on the ground, which was deliberate and highly dangerous. I then issued the player with a
permanent red card.”
ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF OTHER EVIDENCE (e.g. medical reports)
From video clips:
The Player, having received the ball from his scrum half as the first runner off a ruck, moved the ball
on quickly to the man outside him (#10). The opponent (Brazil #16) had been preparing to make a
front on tackle on the Player and was in a good low body position to do so, but continued to make the
tackle even although the ball had left the hands of the Player.
The tackler’s initial contact on the Player was to the outside of his right leg, the Player then having
turned side on to the tackler as he had pivoted that way as he made his pass to #10. The Player was
brought to the ground as the tackler slid downwards on the Player’s legs, ending up around, and
holding, his ankles.
By then the ball had been passed on and the tackle was late.
The Player ended up with his front of body towards the ground, both hands on the ground and with
both feet on the ground, with the tackler’s hands initially still on or around the Player’s ankles.
The Committee observes that with both hands on the ground and with both feet on the ground, the
Player was in a position to stand up, by drawing his feet forward and pushing up from his hands, if his
legs had been free to be moved.
With his left foot on the ground, the Player with his right foot now freed and without looking behind
him, lifted the right foot some height off the ground and at the same time propelled that foot, with
the sole and studs leading, in the direction of the opponent, making contact with the left side of the
opponent’s neck.
The opponent is seen to clutch at that area of his neck; whilst the Player replaces his right foot on the
ground (the left foot had stayed on the ground) and stands up and resumes play.
The photographs of the opponent’s neck show some abrasions to the side of the neck, lower down
the neck towards the shoulder area, consistent with stud marks. No other injury appears to have been
sustained.
251116 Disciplinary Decision Berguet (Belgium) FQT Page 2 of 7

SUMMARY OF PLAYER’S EVIDENCE
The Player’s written explanation follows verbatim:
“1. I was tackled from behind and held by the Brazil player despite no longer being in possession of
the ball.
2.My sole intention was to return to play as quickly as possible, and my immediate reaction was to
free my legs from his grip.
3. I had no visibility of the opponent’s body position, and therefore no deliberate or reckless intention
to make contact with him.
4. Immediately after the match, I approached the opponent to apologise. His words, as well as the
handshake and the embrace we exchanged, made it very clear that he viewed the incident as part of
normal play and not as foul play (refer to video attached).
5. Since I started playing rugby, I have never received a red card.
For these reasons, I respectfully submit that my action does not meet the threshold for a red card, and
I humbly ask to be allowed to participate on Tuesday in what is the most important match of my rugby
career.”
He was examined by the Committee members on this account, particularly on his points 1-3 inclusive.
Under that examination he candidly told the Committee that he was ashamed that he had reacted in
the way that he had and that he had “reacted the wrong way” in trying to get himself released from
being held by his ankles as quickly as possible. He said that he had no intent to injure or hurt the
opponent but just wanted to be let go.
He told the Committee that there was no excuse for acting in the way that he did and that he should
not have done so.
FINDINGS OF FACT
The matters already set out in the sections above as to what can be seen in the video clips and the
Player’s evidence suffice to set out the Committee’s conclusions. The Committee did not accept the
Player’s contentions in his point 3 above – the kicking action by him was deliberately made and made
recklessly as to the potential consequences which could (and did) follow.
In the end, it matters not that the opponent’s tackle was late; frustrated reactions cannot be
countenanced or allowed; especially when a reaction is performed by a kick which makes contact onto
an unprotected neck. Fortunately, no serious injury resulted, which may speak to the extent of actual
force involved.
On the balance of probabilities, the Committee finds that this was an intentional kicking out by the
Player in the direction of where there was a known opponent, carrying with it the very real risk, if not
certainty as it turned out, that contact would be made with the opponent. In his own words his action
taken, in kicking up and back, “was to free my legs from his grip.” And that action constituted physical
abuse of an opponent.
The Player knew (and effectively acknowledged this in his evidence when being questioned by the
Committee) that there was a real risk of the sort of contact which did occur, but in his heated
(over)reaction took that risk anyway.
251116 Disciplinary Decision Berguet (Belgium) FQT Page 3 of 7

DECISION
DECISIONS:
1. The Player accepts that there was foul play but disputed that a Red Card was warranted.
2. By a combination of WR Reg. 17.15.3 and 17.16.1(b) the Player had the onus to show that the Referee
was wrong to issue a Red Card and that this Committee must not make a finding contrary to the Referee’s
decision unless the Committee was satisfied on the balance of probabilities that the Referee’s decision
was wrong.
3. The Player has not satisfied the onus upon him; on the contrary this Committee is adamantly of the view
that the Referee’s decision was the correct one and the only one that could have been made in these
circumstances.
4. However, the Referee, having concluded that the Player’s action was an intentional kick, should have
considered the Player’s foul play as being a breach of Law 9.12 (physical abuse by kicking) rather than a
breach of Law 9.11 (a reckless or dangerous action).
5. The Committee discussed this with the Player and determined that amending the alleged foul play
offence to one of physical abuse by kicking (Law 9.12) could be made by it without causing injustice
(pursuant to WR Reg. 17.26.2), prior notice having been given to the Player and submissions heard on his
behalf. An intentional kick was, and at all times remained, the fundamental factual allegation leading to
the Red Card. Nothing changed in that regard; the same basis remained. A charge more appropriate was
substituted.
6. On that amended charge the Committee upheld the Red Card – it was warranted for an intentional kick,
carried out with recklessness as to the nearness of his opponent, and that opponent’s head and neck, and
the possible consequences.
